relevance_reason: Reports a novel rare TOR1A missense variant (F205I) in a patient with late-onset focal dystonia, with functional cellular studies compared with the DYT1 deltaGAG mutation; this adds supporting evidence on the TOR1A/DYT1 phenotype spectrum.

findings.statement: Calakos et al. (2010) reported a man in his fifth decade of life who had had involuntary jaw movements and grimacing for 3 years, consistent with oromandibular dystonia. He had bipolar disorder treated with lithium, remote exposure to dopamine receptor-blocking agents, cogwheel tone without rigidity, a mild action/postural tremor of the upper extremities, and absent Achilles reflexes. Brain MRI and laboratory studies were normal. His family history was negative for dystonia but included tremor and depression, and the movements responded well to anticholinergic agents.
quotes: The patient was in his fifth decade of life when he reported involuntary jaw movements and grimacing beginning 3 years prior.
Neurological examination revealed an orofacial movement, primarily involving jaw retraction, consistent with an oromandibular dystonia.
The patient’s family history was negative for a history of dystonia, but did include tremor and depression.

findings.statement: In a man with late-onset focal (oromandibular) dystonia, Calakos et al. (2010) sequenced TOR1A and found a heterozygous novel missense mutation in exon 3, c.613T>A (p.F205I). The variant was not present in 800 population controls (1,600 chromosomes). It affects a highly conserved phenylalanine in a beta strand of the AAA domain, and SIFT predicted it to be pathogenic (score 0.03). The authors suggested that the variant may contribute to the expression of dystonia.
quotes: This case report describes an individual with a novel mutation in exon 3 of TOR1A that changed a phenylalanine to isoleucine (c.613T>A, p.F205I). This variant was not identified in 800 anonymized population controls (1600 chromosomes).
The phenylalanine at position 205 is highly conserved across species and is part of a highly conserved beta strand motif in the AAA domain (Figure 1B).
Such an analysis of the F205I mutation yielded a score of 0.03 indicating likely pathogenicity.

findings.statement: Calakos et al. (2010) expressed EGFP-tagged TOR1A in BHK cells. Inclusions formed in 44% of cells expressing the F205I mutant, 79% expressing deltaE, and 10% expressing wildtype. F205I inclusions were larger than deltaE inclusions and colocalized mostly with the ER marker KDEL (96%) rather than the nuclear envelope marker LaminB1 (19%), whereas deltaE inclusions colocalized with LaminB1 (89%). The authors concluded that F205I impairs TOR1A function but that its pathophysiology probably differs from that of deltaE.
quotes: In contrast to wildtype TOR1A-EGFP, F205I-TOR1A-EGFP frequently produced inclusions in transfected cells (44% F205I vs. 10% wildtype; p<0.05).

F205I mutant TOR1A, in contrast to the pronounced colocalization of ΔE TOR1A with nuclear envelope markers, preferentially colocalized with the ER marker, KDEL (96%, n=67 cells) relative to Lamin B1 (19%, n=41 cells).
the ΔE mutant TOR1A produced inclusions in a significantly greater fraction of transfected cells (79% ΔE vs. 44% F205I; p<0.05)

findings.statement: Calakos et al. (2010) suggested that the cellular differences between the F205I and deltaE TOR1A mutants may reflect the milder clinical phenotype (late-onset focal dystonia) of the patient carrying F205I, compared with the early-onset generalized dystonia caused by deltaGAG.
quotes: we also identified differences suggesting that the pathophysiology of F205I mutant TOR1A is unlikely to be identical to that caused by the ΔE mutant TOR1A; an observation possibly reflective of the milder clinical phenotype in which the F205I mutation was identified.

relevance_reason: PET imaging study showing reduced striatal and thalamic D2 receptor availability in DYT1 mutation carriers (manifesting and nonmanifesting), compared with DYT6; pathophysiologic evidence for DYT1.

findings.statement: Carbon et al. (2009) used [11C]raclopride PET to study manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of the DYT1 and DYT6 dystonia mutations and found significant reductions in caudate and putamen D2 receptor availability in both groups of mutation carriers relative to healthy controls. The reductions were greater in DYT6 than in DYT1 carriers (-38.0% vs -15.0%), and there was no significant difference between manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of either genotype.
quotes: Significant reductions in caudate and putamen D(2) receptor availability were evident in both groups of mutation carriers relative to healthy controls (p < 0.001).

The changes were greater in DYT6 relative to DYT1 carriers (-38.0 +/- 3.0% vs -15.0 +/- 3.0%, p < 0.001). By contrast, there was no significant difference between manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of either genotype.

phenotypes.text: reduced striatal D2 receptor availability on raclopride PET

findings.statement: Carbon et al. (2009) found by voxel-based analysis reduced raclopride binding in the ventrolateral thalamus of both DYT1 and DYT6 mutation carriers, more pronounced in DYT6 carriers and not influenced by clinical manifestation. The authors concluded that reduced D2 receptor availability is compatible with dysfunction or loss of D2-bearing neurons, increased synaptic dopamine, or both, and likely represents a susceptibility factor for developing clinical manifestations in mutation carriers.
quotes: Voxel-based analysis confirmed these findings and additionally revealed reduced RAC binding in the ventrolateral thalamus of both groups of mutation carriers.
Reduced D(2) receptor availability in carriers of dystonia genes is compatible with dysfunction or loss of D(2)-bearing neurons, increased synaptic dopamine levels, or both.
are likely to represent susceptibility factors for the development of clinical manifestations in mutation carriers.

relevance_reason: Describes a Dutch family with primary focal dystonia in which DYT1 (TOR1A) mutations were excluded and linkage to other DYT loci was not found. This is evidence of genetic heterogeneity, not a characterization of DYT1 itself.

findings.statement: Contarino et al. (2008) described a large 3-generation Dutch family from a small village on a former island with primary focal dystonia. Of the 24 family members examined, 8 were definitely affected and 4 were possibly affected. Mutations in the DYT1 gene and the SGCE gene were not detected, and linkage to the DYT6, DYT7, DYT13 and DYT16 loci was excluded, indicating genetic heterogeneity.
quotes: Eight definitely affected and four possibly affected subjects were detected.
Mutations in DYT1 gene and in the epsilon-sarcoglycan (SGCE) genes were not detected. We could not find linkage to the dominant DYT6, DYT7, DYT13, or the recessive DYT16 loci.

findings.statement: In the Dutch focal dystonia family reported by Contarino et al. (2008), the affected members had mild cranio-cervical-brachial dystonia. Mean age at onset was 45.5 years (range, 39 to 56 years), the mean BFMDRS motor score was 4.4 (range, 1 to 8), and the mean TWSTRS part I score was 11.3 (range, 8 to 23).
quotes: Clinical presentation consisted of mild cranio-cervical-brachial dystonia. Mean age at onset was 45.5 years (range, 39-56).
Mean BFMDRS motor score was 4.4 (range, 1-8). Mean TWSTRS score (part I) was 11.3 (range, 8-23).

relevance_reason: The title reports that the TOR1A D216H polymorphism changes how likely European patients are to develop DYT1 dystonia. This is evidence about reduced penetrance and a genetic modifier of the disorder.

findings.statement: Kamm et al. (2008) reported that the D216H polymorphism modified susceptibility to DYT1 dystonia in European patients.
quotes: Susceptibility to DYT1 dystonia in European patients is modified by the D216H polymorphism.

relevance_reason: Reports a novel TOR1A missense variant (p.Arg288Gln) in a patient with early-onset DYT1 dystonia, with functional studies.

findings.statement: In a patient with early-onset DYT1 dystonia, Zirn et al. (2008) identified a c.863G>A transition in exon 5 of the TOR1A gene by sequencing, resulting in an arg288-to-gln (p.Arg288Gln) substitution in subdomain alpha-5 of TOR1A. The change was absent from 1,000 control chromosomes, and Arg288 is conserved throughout vertebrate evolution. The authors suggested that this may be a novel pathogenic TOR1A mutation in DYT1.
quotes: Detection of sequence change c.863G>A in exon 5 of TOR1A in the patient. The G>A transition results in an exchange of an arginine for glutamine (p.Arg288Gln) in subdomain alpha5 of TOR1A.
The base change is absent in 1000 control chromosomes; an Arg at position 288 of TOR1A has been conserved throughout vertebrate evolution
The sequence change described here may be a novel pathogenic mutation of TOR1A in DYT1.

findings.statement: Zirn et al. (2008) found that HEK293 cells overexpressing TOR1A with the p.Arg288Gln mutation showed an enlarged perinuclear space, the same morphologic change seen in cells overexpressing the common delta-GAG TOR1A mutation but not in cells overexpressing wildtype TOR1A.
quotes: functional studies demonstrate enlarged perinuclear space in HEK293 cells overexpressing TOR1A with the p.Arg288Gln mutation. The same morphological changes are observed in cells overexpressing the common triangle upGAG TOR1A mutation but not in cells overexpressing wild-type TOR1A.

relevance_reason: Nationwide French census of TOR1A mutation carriers with haplotype analysis and disease/mutation frequency estimates for DYT1.

findings.statement: Frédéric et al. (2008) carried out a nationwide census of French TOR1A mutation carriers, studying 53 index cases and 104 relatives. They estimated the disease frequency of early-onset torsion dystonia due to TOR1A in France at 0.13 per 100,000 and the mutation frequency at 0.17 per 100,000, and concluded that the disease is rare in France.
quotes: Overall, 53 index cases and 104 relatives were studied and haplotypes linked to the mutation constructed.
This study demonstrates the scarcity of this disease in France with estimated disease frequency of 0.13:100,000 and mutation frequency of 0.17:100,000.

findings.statement: In haplotype analysis of 53 French families carrying the recurrent TOR1A mutation, Frédéric et al. (2008) found the previously reported Ashkenazi Jewish haplotype in 11 families. The remaining families carried distinct haplotypes, which the authors suggested reflected independent mutation events.
quotes: The previously reported Ashkenazi-Jewish haplotype was found in 11 families with the remainder carrying distinct haplotypes suggesting independent mutation events.

variants.as_reported: unique and recurrent mutation in the TOR1A gene

findings.population: French; Ashkenazi Jewish haplotype in 11 families

relevance_reason: Identifies the D216H polymorphism in TOR1A/DYT1 as a modifier of penetrance of the GAG deletion in DYT1 dystonia.

findings.statement: Risch et al. (2007) genotyped 3 DYT1 SNPs, including the coding variant D216H, in DYT1 GAG-deletion carriers with dystonia (n=119), GAG-deletion carriers without dystonia (n=113), and controls (n=197). Compared with controls, the 216H allele was more frequent in nonmanifesting carriers and less frequent in carriers with dystonia. In haplotype analysis, the H allele in trans with the GAG deletion was highly protective, and there was suggestive evidence that the D216 allele in cis is required for the disease to be penetrant. The authors concluded that this was the first clinically relevant gene modifier of DYT1.
quotes: We tested DYT1 GAG-deletion carriers with (n=119) and without (n=113) clinical signs of dystonia and control individuals (n=197) and found the frequency of the 216H allele to be increased in GAG-deletion carriers without dystonia and to be decreased in carriers with dystonia, compared with the control individuals.

Analysis of haplotypes demonstrated a highly protective effect of the H allele in trans with the GAG deletion; there was also suggestive evidence that the D216 allele in cis is required for the disease to be penetrant.

findings.statement: Risch et al. (2007) noted that the DYT1 GAG deletion is a major cause of early-onset dystonia, but only 30% of mutation carriers express clinical disease.
quotes: A GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene is a major cause of early-onset dystonia, but clinical disease expression occurs in only 30% of mutation carriers.

relevance_reason: Describes a Serbian family with the DYT1 GAG deletion showing variable expressivity and reduced penetrance, plus dystonia in family members who do not carry the deletion.

findings.statement: Kostić et al. (2006) described a large Serbian family in which the DYT1 phenotype varied widely within the family, from asymptomatic carrier status to late-onset focal dystonia and generalized jerky dystonia.
quotes: We describe a large Serbian family with significant intrafamilial variability of the DYT1 phenotype, from asymptomatic carrier status to late-onset focal, and generalized jerky dystonia.

findings.statement: In a large Serbian family, Kostić et al. (2006) identified 7 carriers of the 3-bp (GAG) deletion in the DYT1 gene. Six carriers were confirmed by direct analysis and 1 was inferred from haplotype. Only 2 of the carriers had dystonia, giving a penetrance of 29%.
quotes: Seven mutation carriers (six proven by direct analysis and one by inferred haplotype) were identified, but only two of them were affected by dystonia (penetrance reduced to 29%).

findings.statement: Kostić et al. (2006) found that 3 members of the same Serbian family who did not carry the GAG deletion also developed dystonia: 2 had multifocal dystonia and 1 had torticollis. The authors suggested that these involuntary movements were caused by some other factor, such as another dystonia gene, or might be psychogenic.
quotes: In addition, three GAG-deletion-negative family members also developed dystonia (two multifocal dystonia and one torticollis), suggesting that their involuntary movements are due to some other etiological factor(s) (i.e., another dystonia gene), or may be psychogenic.

relevance_reason: PET imaging study of non-manifesting DYT1 mutation carriers that shows reduced striatal D2 receptor binding as a trait feature of the genotype; relevant to pathogenesis.

findings.statement: Asanuma et al. (2005) used PET with [11C]-raclopride to study non-manifesting carriers of the DYT1 mutation. Striatal D2 receptor binding was reduced by about 15% in the caudate and putamen (p < 0.005). The authors suggested that reduced striatal D2 binding is a trait feature of the DYT1 genotype.
quotes: the authors used PET and [11C]-raclopride to assess non-manifesting carriers of the DYT1 mutation
D2 receptor binding was reduced by approximately 15% in caudate and putamen (p < 0.005)
These results suggest that striatal D2 binding reductions are a trait feature of the DYT1 genotype.

relevance_reason: Transgenic mouse model overexpressing human DeltaE-torsinA that shows dystonia-like behavior and pathology resembling DYT1.

findings.statement: Shashidharan et al. (2005) generated 4 independent lines of transgenic mice overexpressing human DeltaE-torsinA under a neuron-specific enolase promoter. As early as 3 weeks after birth, the mice developed abnormal involuntary movements with dystonic-appearing self-clasping of the limbs, as well as hyperkinesia and rapid bidirectional circling. About 40% of the transgenic mice in each line showed these severe behavioral abnormalities.
quotes: We generated four independent lines of transgenic mice by overexpressing human DeltaE-torsinA using a neuron specific enolase promoter.

The transgenic mice developed abnormal involuntary movements with dystonic-appearing, self-clasping of limbs, as early as 3 weeks after birth. Animals also showed hyperkinesia and rapid bi-directional circling.
Approximately 40% of transgenic mice from each line demonstrated these severe behavioral abnormalities.

findings.statement: In the DeltaE-torsinA transgenic mice, Shashidharan et al. (2005) found decreased striatal dopamine in behaviorally affected animals but increased levels in transgenic mice without behavioral changes. Immunohistochemistry showed perinuclear inclusions and aggregates that stained for ubiquitin, torsinA, and lamin, a nuclear envelope marker. These inclusions were in neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus and other brainstem regions, in a pattern similar to that described in DYT1 patients.
quotes: Neurochemical analyses revealed decreases in striatal dopamine in affected transgenic mice, although levels were increased in those that had no behavioral changes.
Immunohistochemistry demonstrated perinuclear inclusions and aggregates that stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA and lamin, a marker of the nuclear envelope.
Inclusions were detected in neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus and in other brain stem regions in a pattern similar to what has been described in DYT1 patients.

relevance_reason: Postmortem neuropathology study of genetically confirmed DYT1 dystonia patients describing brainstem inclusions; supports pathogenesis section.

findings.statement: McNaught et al. (2004) described perinuclear inclusion bodies in the midbrain reticular formation and periaqueductal gray in 4 clinically documented and genetically confirmed DYT1 patients but not in controls. The inclusions were located within cholinergic and other neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus, cuneiform nucleus, and griseum centrale mesencephali, and stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA, and the nuclear envelope protein lamin A/C. No inclusion bodies were detected in the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatum, hippocampus, or selected regions of the cerebral cortex.
quotes: We describe, for the first time to our knowledge, perinuclear inclusion bodies in the midbrain reticular formation and periaqueductal gray in four clinically documented and genetically confirmed DYT1 patients but not in controls.

The inclusions were located within cholinergic and other neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus, cuneiform nucleus, and griseum centrale mesencephali and stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA, and the nuclear envelope protein lamin A/C.
No evidence of inclusion body formation was detected in the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatum, hippocampus, or selected regions of the cerebral cortex.

phenotypes.text: perinuclear inclusion bodies in midbrain reticular formation and periaqueductal gray

findings.statement: McNaught et al. (2004) also noted tau/ubiquitin-immunoreactive aggregates in pigmented neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta and locus ceruleus in all 4 DYT1 dystonia cases but not in controls. The authors concluded that the findings supported the notion that DYT1 dystonia is associated with impaired protein handling and the nuclear envelope, and suggested that alterations in the pedunculopontine and cuneiform nuclei and related brainstem structures, which mediate motor activity and muscle tone, could underlie the pathophysiology of DYT1 dystonia.
quotes: We also noted tau/ubiquitin-immunoreactive aggregates in pigmented neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta and locus coeruleus in all four DYT1 dystonia cases, but not in controls.
This study supports the notion that DYT1 dystonia is associated with impaired protein handling and the nuclear envelope.
suggests that alterations in these structures could underlie the pathophysiology of DYT1 dystonia

phenotypes.text: tau/ubiquitin-immunoreactive aggregates in substantia nigra and locus ceruleus neurons

relevance_reason: The paper reports that carriers of the DYT1 GAG mutation have a higher risk of recurrent major depression, which adds a psychiatric feature to the DYT1 phenotype.

findings.statement: Heiman et al. (2004) gave a standardized psychiatric interview to members of families with an identified DYT1 mutation. They compared 96 mutation carriers with dystonia, 60 carriers without dystonia, and 65 noncarriers. Compared with noncarriers, the risk of recurrent major depressive disorder was higher in nonmanifesting carriers (RR = 4.95, CI 1.72-14.29) and in manifesting carriers (RR = 3.62, CI 1.00-10.53). Carriers also developed recurrent depression at an earlier age.
quotes: The authors classified family members into three groups: mutation carriers with dystonia (manifesting carriers; n = 96), mutation carriers without dystonia (non-manifesting carriers; n = 60), and noncarriers (n = 65).

The risk for recurrent major depressive disorder was increased in both non-manifesting carriers (RR = 4.95, CI = 1.72 to 14.29) and manifesting carriers (RR = 3.62, CI = 1.00 to 10.53) compared with noncarriers.
Mutation carriers also had earlier age at onset of recurrent major depressive disorder than noncarriers.

findings.statement: Heiman et al. (2004) found that how severe the motor signs were did not predict the likelihood of recurrent depression in DYT1 mutation carriers. Carriers did not have a higher risk of other affective disorders, such as single major depression or bipolar disorder. The authors concluded that early-onset recurrent major depression is associated with the DYT1 GAG mutation independently of motor symptoms, and suggested that it is a clinical expression of the mutation.
quotes: The severity of motor signs was not associated with the likelihood of recurrent depression. Mutation carriers did not have an increased risk for other affective disorders, such as single major depression or bipolar disorder.
Early-onset recurrent major depression is associated with the DYT1 GAG mutation and this association is independent of motor manifestations of dystonia.
These findings suggest that early-onset recurrent depression is a clinical expression of the DYT1 gene mutation.

relevance_reason: Diffusion tensor imaging study showing that DYT1 mutation carriers have microstructural white matter changes, which helps explain how the disease develops.

findings.statement: Carbon et al. (2004) used diffusion tensor MRI to study white matter pathways in DYT1 mutation carriers and control subjects. Fractional anisotropy, a measure of axonal integrity and coherence, was reduced (p < 0.005) in the subgyral white matter of the sensorimotor cortex of DYT1 carriers. The authors suggested that abnormal anatomical connectivity of the supplementary motor area may contribute to the susceptibility of DYT1 carriers to develop clinical manifestations of dystonia.
quotes: Fractional anisotropy (FA), a measure of axonal integrity and coherence, was reduced (p < 0.005) in the subgyral white matter of the sensorimotor cortex of DYT1 carriers.
Abnormal anatomical connectivity of the supplementary motor area may contribute to the susceptibility of DYT1 carriers to develop clinical manifestations of dystonia.

phenotypes.text: reduced fractional anisotropy in sensorimotor subgyral white matter

relevance_reason: FDG PET imaging study of manifesting and nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers, showing metabolic patterns related to penetrance and genotype; adds pathophysiologic evidence for DYT1.

findings.statement: Carbon et al. (2004) used FDG PET to scan 12 nonmanifesting and 11 manifesting DYT1 gene carriers, 6 nonmanifesting and 7 manifesting DYT6 gene carriers, and 11 controls. Manifesting carriers of both genotypes showed bilateral hypermetabolism in the presupplementary motor area (Brodmann area 6) and parietal association cortices (BA 40/7) compared with nonmanifesting counterparts, whereas DYT1 carriers showed genotype-specific increases in metabolism in the putamen, anterior cingulate (BA 24/32), and cerebellar hemispheres. The authors suggested that clinical manifestations are related to cortical dysfunction, while subcortical metabolic abnormalities may represent genotype-specific trait features, and that dystonia may be associated with abnormal movement preparation caused by defective sensorimotor integration.
quotes: FDG PET was used to scan 12 nonmanifesting and 11 manifesting DYT1 gene carriers, 6 nonmanifesting DYT6 gene carriers and 7 manifesting DYT6 gene carriers, as well as 11 control subjects.

Manifesting gene carriers of both genotypes exhibited bilateral hypermetabolism in the presupplementary motor area (Brodmann area [BA] 6) and parietal association cortices (BA 40/7) compared with the respective nonmanifesting counterparts. By contrast, genotype-specific increases in metabolism were found in the putamen, anterior cingulate (BA 24/32), and cerebellar hemispheres of DYT1 carriers.

Whereas clinical manifestations are related to cortical dysfunction, metabolic abnormalities in subcortical structures may represent trait features that are specific for individual dystonia genotypes.

phenotypes.text: hypermetabolism in presupplementary motor area and parietal association cortex in manifesting carriers
increased metabolism in putamen, anterior cingulate, and cerebellar hemispheres

findings.statement: Carbon et al. (2004) found that, in contrast to DYT1 carriers, genotype-specific changes in DYT6 carriers involved hypometabolism of the putamen and hypermetabolism in the temporal cortex (BA 21), indicating distinct subcortical metabolic signatures for the 2 dystonia genotypes.
quotes: Genotype-specific changes in DYT6 involved hypometabolism of the putamen and hypermetabolism in the temporal cortex (BA 21).

relevance_reason: The title shows the paper studies dystonia musculorum deformans, the subject of this entry. Only the title was supplied, with no abstract or full text, so no clinical, genetic or inheritance findings can be backed by quotes.

Only the title is available. It shows the paper is about formes frustes (incomplete or mild forms) of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans, which is relevant to DYT1's clinical variability. No patient, family or genetic details are available.

findings.statement: ZEMAN et al. (1960) reported on the formes frustes (incomplete or mild forms) of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans.
quotes: Idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans. II. The formes frustes.

relevance_reason: The title shows this is a study of the hereditary pattern of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans, which is the subject of this entry. Only the title was available, so the actual inheritance conclusions cannot be extracted.

findings.statement: ZEMAN et al. (1959) studied the hereditary pattern of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans.
quotes: Idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans. I. The hereditary pattern.

relevance_reason: Screening of 256 unselected German dystonia patients for the DYT1 GAG deletion; gives mutation frequency and shows the range of phenotypes in carriers.

findings.statement: Grundmann et al. (2003) screened 256 patients with different subtypes of dystonia from 4 movement disorder outpatient clinics in Germany for the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene using PCR. They found the deletion in 6 of the 256 patients.
quotes: Two hundred fifty-six patients were tested for the GAG deletion mutation in the DYT1 gene by means of published primers and polymerase chain reaction amplification to determine GAG deletion status.
Six of the 256 patients did carry the GAG-deletion in the DYT1 gene.

findings.statement: Grundmann et al. (2003) found that only 2 of the 6 GAG deletion carriers had classic early-onset primary generalized dystonia. Two carriers had multifocal dystonia, 1 of them with involvement of cranial and cervical muscles, and 2 had writer's cramp of both hands with only slight progression. The authors concluded that the mutation may be associated with segmental and multifocal as well as generalized dystonia, and that this phenotypic variability may make it difficult to predict carrier status and to give genetic counseling.
quotes: However, only 2 of the 6 mutation carriers presented with what is thought to represent classic features of early-onset primary generalized dystonia.

The DYT1 mutation was also detected in 2 patients with multifocal dystonia, 1 of them presenting with involvement of cranial and cervical muscles, and in 2 patients with writer's cramp of both hands with only slight progression.
A priori prediction of the mutation carrier status in dystonic patients and genetic counseling of affected families with respect to the clinical manifestation may prove difficult.

relevance_reason: Reports impaired sequence learning and abnormal brain activation on PET in nonmanifesting DYT1 mutation carriers, i.e., features in clinically unaffected carriers of the disorder.

findings.statement: Ghilardi et al. (2003) compared movement and sequence learning in 12 clinically unaffected DYT1 mutation carriers with 12 age-matched controls. Motor performance did not differ between groups (no significant differences in movement time or spatial accuracy), but sequence learning was reduced in gene carriers relative to controls (p < 0.01). The authors suggested that abnormalities in motor behavior exist in clinically nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers.
quotes: we compared movement and sequence learning in 12 clinically unaffected DYT1 carriers with 12 age-matched controls

We found that motor performance was similar in the DYT1 and control groups, with no significant differences in movement time and spatial accuracy measured during each of the tasks. In contrast, sequence learning was reduced in gene carriers relative to controls (p < 0.01).

findings.statement: Ghilardi et al. (2003) used H2(15)O PET during task performance in nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers. During motor execution, carriers showed increased activation in the left premotor cortex and right supplementary motor area, with reduced activation in the posterior medial cerebellum; during sequence learning, activation was increased in the left ventral prefrontal cortex and lateral cerebellum. The authors suggested that localized increases in neural activity may enable normal movement execution in carriers but may not compensate for their defect in sequence learning.
quotes: PET imaging during motor execution showed increased activation in gene carriers (p < 0.001, uncorrected) in the left premotor cortex and right supplementary motor area, with concomitant reduction in the posterior medial cerebellum.
During sequence learning, activation responses in DYT1 carriers were increased in the left ventral prefrontal cortex, and lateral cerebellum.
Although localized increases in neural activity may enable normal movement execution in these subjects, this mechanism may not compensate for their defect in sequence learning.

relevance_reason: Evaluates diagnostic classification of dystonia among DYT1 GAG deletion carriers and noncarriers in DYT1 families; relevant to diagnosis/penetrance considerations.

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (2002) evaluated the hierarchical diagnostic categories of definite, probable, and possible dystonia used in family studies by assessing 147 DYT1 GAG deletion carriers and 113 blood-related noncarriers from 43 families. Only the category of definite dystonia was 100% specific; probable dystonia, but not possible dystonia, was increased in carriers compared with noncarriers. The authors recommended that only individuals with definite signs of dystonia be considered affected in linkage and other genetic studies.
quotes: The authors assessed 147 DYT1 GAG deletion carriers and 113 blood-related noncarriers from 43 families. Only the category of definite dystonia was 100% specific.
Probable dystonia, but not possible, was increased in carriers compared with noncarriers.
The authors recommend that only those with definite signs of dystonia be considered affected in linkage and other genetic studies.

relevance_reason: The paper screens Danish probands with primary torsion dystonia for the DYT1 GAG deletion. It reports a de novo mutation and reduced penetrance in sporadic cases.

findings.statement: Hjermind et al. (2002) screened 107 Danish probands with primary torsion dystonia for the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene, after secondary dystonia had been excluded clinically and biochemically. They found the mutation in 3 probands, all of whom had the classical DYT1 phenotype. None of the probands with other types of dystonia carried the GAG deletion.
quotes: Mutation analyses for the GAG-deletion in the DYT1 gene were performed on 107 probands; and the mutation was detected in three.
All three probands had the classical phenotype of DYT1-dystonia, but only one had a family history of dystonia.
None of the probands in our study with other types of dystonia had the GAG-deletion as reported in other studies.

findings.statement: Hjermind et al. (2002) described 2 of the 3 Danish DYT1 GAG-deletion carriers who were apparently sporadic cases. In one, the mutation had arisen de novo. In the other, a parent was an asymptomatic carrier. The authors noted that de novo mutations in the DYT1 gene are seldom reported, although independent founder mutations are known to have occurred.
quotes: The other two probands had, obviously, sporadic DYT1-dystonia, one of which was caused by a de novo mutation, while the other one had a parent being an asymptomatic carrier.
De novo mutations in the DYT1 gene are seldom reported although independent founder mutations are known to have occurred.

findings.statement: Hjermind et al. (2002) found DYT1 dystonia to be uncommon among Danish probands with primary torsion dystonia (3 of 107), even though several probands had early-onset generalized dystonia.
quotes: The frequency of DYT1-dystonia was low in our study even though several probands had early onset generalised dystonia.

relevance_reason: A review of the genetics of primary dystonias. The abstract names idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1) as one of the conditions discussed but reports no patients, variants or data specific to DYT1.

findings.statement: In a review, Németh (2002) described the dystonias as a heterogeneous group of disorders with a strong inherited basis. The review covered primary dystonias, including idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1), as well as 'dystonia-plus' syndromes and heredodegenerative disorders, with a focus on their clinical and genetic features and molecular mechanisms.
quotes: Dystonias are a heterogeneous group of disorders which are known to have a strong inherited basis.
Conditions discussed in detail include idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1), focal dystonias (DYT7) and mixed dystonias (DYT6 and DYT13)

relevance_reason: Reports a novel 18-bp in-frame deletion in TOR1A in a patient with atypical early onset dystonia with myoclonic features, and screening of patients with dystonia and early onset parkinsonism.

findings.statement: Leung et al. (2001) found an 18-bp deletion in the TOR1A gene (Phe323_Tyr328del) in a patient with early onset dystonia and myoclonic features. The deletion was predicted to remove 6 amino acids close to the carboxy terminus of torsinA, including a putative phosphorylation site. The authors stated that this was the first TOR1A mutation identified besides the GAG deletion (Glu302/303del), and that it was associated with a distinct type of early onset dystonia.
quotes: An 18-bp deletion (Phe323_Tyr328del) in the TOR1A gene was found in a patient with early onset dystonia and myoclonic features.
This deletion would remove 6 amino acids close to the carboxy terminus, including a putative phosphorylation site of torsinA.
This 18-bp deletion is the first additional mutation, beyond the GAG-deletion (Glu302/303del), to be found in the TOR1A gene, and is associated with a distinct type of early onset dystonia.

findings.statement: Leung et al. (2001) screened TOR1A in 40 patients with early onset dystonia or early onset parkinsonism (EOP) and found 3 variations, none in EOP patients. Two infrequent intronic single-bp changes of unknown consequence were found in a dystonia patient and in the mother of an EOP patient.
quotes: In a screen of 40 patients, we identified three variations, none of which occurred in EOP patients.
Two infrequent intronic single base pair (bp) changes of unknown consequences were found in a dystonia patient and the mother of an EOP patient.

relevance_reason: This is a haplotype study of patients who carry the DYT1 GAG deletion. It gives population-genetic evidence on founder effects in Ashkenazi Jewish and non-Jewish British patients with DYT1 dystonia.

findings.statement: Valente et al. (1999) analyzed haplotypes around the DYT1 gene in 9 Ashkenazi Jewish (AJ) British patients with the GAG deletion. All of them carried the same haplotype as North American AJ patients. The authors took this as support for the theory that the current British AJ community descends from the same small group of individuals as North American Jewry.
quotes: we analysed the haplotypes surrounding DYT1 in 9 AJ and 15 non-Jewish British patients carrying the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene

We found that all AJ British patients carried the same haplotype as the North American Jews, sustaining the theory that the current British AJ community descends from the same small group of individuals as the North American Jewry.

findings.statement: Among 15 non-Jewish British patients with the DYT1 GAG deletion, Valente et al. (1999) found only a limited number of distinct founder haplotypes. They concluded that the GAG deletion is not a very frequent mutation and has arisen only a limited number of times over the centuries.
quotes: Furthermore, in the non-Jewish British patients, only a limited number of distinct founder mutations was observed.
This supports the hypothesis that the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene is not a very frequent mutation, and that it has arisen only a limited number of times throughout the centuries.

relevance_reason: A review of primary dystonias. It only mentions DYT1 mapping to 9q34 and mutations in an ATP-binding protein gene, and it proposes the dystonia 1-12 nomenclature.

findings.statement: In a review of the clinical and molecular genetics of primary dystonias, Müller et al. (1998) proposed naming the known forms dystonias 1-12. They noted that most of these forms can be told apart by genetic criteria, with autosomal dominant idiopathic torsion dystonia designated DYT1.
quotes: proposes referring to the known forms, most of which can be distinguished by genetic criteria, as dystonias 1-12

findings.statement: Müller et al. (1998) reviewed the gene loci found in autosomal dominant primary dystonias, including idiopathic torsion dystonia on 9q34. They also reported that mutations in a gene coding for an ATP-binding protein had been detected in idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1).
quotes: To date gene loci have been identified in at least six autosomal dominant forms, i.e., in idiopathic torsion dystonia (9q34)
Mutations in a gene coding for an ATP-binding protein were detected in idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1)

relevance_reason: Case report of a Japanese patient with primary torsion dystonia carrying the DYT1 3-bp (GAG) deletion. Only the title was available.

findings.statement: Ikeuchi et al. (1999) reported a Japanese patient with primary torsion dystonia who carried the 3-bp (GAG) deletion in the DYT1 gene. The authors described the patient's clinical presentation as unique.
quotes: A case of primary torsion dystonia in Japan with the 3-bp (GAG) deletion in the DYT1 gene with a unique clinical presentation.

relevance_reason: Mutation screening of the DYT1 GAG deletion in German patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia. It adds evidence on how often the deletion occurs in different clinical subtypes.

findings.statement: Kamm et al. (1999) screened 57 German patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia for the 3-bp GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene. They found it in 3 of 5 patients with early limb-onset dystonia, one of whom had a positive family history, and in 1 young patient with multifocal dystonia and a short disease course.
quotes: We examined 57 patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) for the 3-bp GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene on human chromosome 9q34.

Three of five patients with early limb-onset ITD, one of them with a positive family history, tested positive for the mutation, as did one young patient with multifocal dystonia and a short course of the disease.

findings.statement: Kamm et al. (1999) did not find the GAG deletion in 2 patients with early-onset generalized dystonia that began in the cervical muscles, or in 5 other patients with multifocal, 14 with segmental, and 30 with focal cervical dystonia. They suggested that in their population the deletion accounts for a major portion of typical early limb-onset dystonia but not for other types of dystonia.
quotes: Two patients with early-onset generalized dystonia beginning in the cervical muscles, as well as five other patients with multifocal, 14 patients with segmental, and 30 patients with focal cervical dystonia did not carry the mutation.
This suggests that the GAG deletion is responsible for a major portion of cases of typical early limb-onset dystonia, but not for other types of dystonia, in our population.

phenotypes.text: early-onset generalized dystonia with cervical onset

relevance_reason: The paper identifies the DYT1 gene (encoding torsinA) on 9q34 and the recurrent 3-bp deletion that causes early-onset torsion dystonia.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) identified the DYT1 gene on chromosome 9q34 as the gene responsible for autosomal dominant early-onset torsion dystonia. They found that almost all cases of early-onset dystonia carried a unique 3-bp deletion, which results in loss of one of a pair of glutamic acid residues in a conserved region of torsinA, a novel ATP-binding protein. The deletion appeared to have arisen independently in different ethnic populations.
quotes: This study identifies the DYT1 gene on human chromosome 9q34 as being responsible for this dominant disease.
Almost all cases of early-onset dystonia have a unique 3-bp deletion that appears to have arisen idependently in different ethnic populations.
This deletion results in loss of one of a pair of glutamic-acid residues in a conserved region of a novel ATP-binding protein, termed torsinA.

variants.as_reported: 3-bp deletion resulting in loss of one of a pair of glutamic-acid residues

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) concluded that the recurrent 3-bp DYT1 deletion appeared to have arisen independently in different ethnic populations.
quotes: Almost all cases of early-onset dystonia have a unique 3-bp deletion that appears to have arisen idependently in different ethnic populations.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) described early-onset torsion dystonia as a movement disorder that begins in childhood and is characterized by twisting muscle contractures. Symptoms were believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia.
quotes: Early-onset torsion dystonia is a movement disorder, characterized by twisting muscle contractures, that begins in childhood.
Symptoms are believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) found that torsinA, the DYT1 gene product, is a novel ATP-binding protein. It has homologs in nematode, rat, mouse and humans and shows some resemblance to the heat-shock protein and Clp protease families.
quotes: This protein has homologues in nematode, rat, mouse and humans, with some resemblance to the family of heat-shock proteins and Clp proteases.

relevance_reason: Fine mapping of the DYT1 locus on 9q34 through a YAC contig and linkage disequilibrium analysis of the Ashkenazi Jewish founder mutation.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) built a YAC contig covering 600 kb of the 2-cM region between D9S62a and ASS on chromosome 9q34. They added new polymorphic loci to the linkage disequilibrium analysis of the Ashkenazi Jewish founder mutation and placed the DYT1 gene most likely within a 150-kb region between D9S2161 and D9S63.
quotes: A YAC contig has now been created spanning 600 kb of this region including D9S62a.
The location of the DYT1 gene has been refined within this contig using several new polymorphic loci to expand the linkage disequilibrium analysis of the AJ founder mutation.
The most likely location of the DYT1 gene is within a 150 kb region between the loci D9S2161 and D9S63.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) stated that early-onset torsion dystonia due to DYT1 is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with reduced penetrance of 30 to 40%. They noted that DYT1 appears to account for most cases of early-onset torsion dystonia in both Ashkenazi Jewish and non-Jewish families.
quotes: This disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant mode with reduced penetrance (30%-40%).
The DYT1 gene, which maps to chromosome 9q34, appears to be responsible for most cases of early-onset torsion dystonia in both Ashkenazic Jewish (AJ) and non-Jewish families.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) noted that the abnormal involuntary movements of torsion dystonia are believed to be caused by unbalanced neural transmission in the basal ganglia.
quotes: The abnormal involuntary movements associated with this disease are believed to be caused by unbalanced neural transmission in the basal ganglia.

relevance_reason: The paper describes adult-onset idiopathic cranial or cervical dystonia, not early-onset DYT1 torsion dystonia. It reports clinical anticipation and suggests a trinucleotide repeat mechanism, which is useful context about the genetics of dystonia and its heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Cheng et al. (1996) studied 260 probands with idiopathic adult-onset cranial or cervical dystonia. Their mean age at onset was 45.71 +/- 15.85 years. Forty-nine probands had a positive family history of dystonia or tremor in first- or second-degree relatives, and 7 had affected siblings only. Postural or action tremor was frequent in patients and relatives, which the authors took as evidence that tremor is part of the clinical manifestation of dystonia.
quotes: we studied the age of onset and family history of 260 patients (probands) with idiopathic adult-onset dystonia (IAD), cranial or cervical. The mean age at onset of these patients was (45.71 +/- 15.85) years.
Forty-nine probands had a positive family history of dystonia or tremor in first- and second-degree relatives, and 7 had affected siblings only.
The significance of tremor as a part of clinical manifestation of dystonia was evidenced by a high frequency of postural or action tremor in patients and relatives.

findings.statement: In a retrospective analysis of 49 families with adult-onset cranial or cervical dystonia, Cheng et al. (1996) found that age at onset was on average 21.25 years earlier in the second generation than in the first (p = 1.11 x 10(-8)). The authors suggested that this was compatible with genetic anticipation and that an unstable trinucleotide repeat is most likely involved in adult-onset primary cranial or cervical dystonia.
quotes: Age of onset of clinical symptoms was earlier, by an average of 21.25 years, in the second generation than in the first generation.
The mean age at onset of affected family members differed significantly between successive generations in these 49 families (p = 1.11 x 10(-8)).
These findings are most compatible with genetic anticipation and suggest that an unstable trinucleotide repeat is most likely involved in adult-onset primary cranial or cervical dystonia.

relevance_reason: Haplotype analysis at the DYT1 locus in Ashkenazi Jewish patients with focal occupational hand dystonia found no DYT1 founder haplotype. This bears on heterogeneity and on whether DYT1 plays a role in focal dystonia.

findings.statement: Gasser et al. (1996) determined haplotypes at 5 marker loci closely linked to DYT1 on chromosome 9q in 10 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with focal hand dystonia (8 with musician's cramp and 2 with writer's cramp). The founder haplotype associated with more than 90% of generalized dystonia cases in the Ashkenazi Jewish population could not be constructed from any of the 20 chromosomes, and no common haplotype was seen. The authors concluded that these findings argued against a role for the DYT1 founder mutation in occupational hand dystonia in this population. They also concluded that if DYT1 is involved in these later-onset dystonias, there was no evidence for a common mutation.
quotes: Genetic haplotypes at five marker loci that are closely linked to the DYT1 gene on chromosome 9q were determined in 10 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with focal hand dystonia (eight with musician's cramp, two with writer's cramp).
The founder haplotype associated with > 90% of cases generalized dystonia in the Ashkenazi Jewish population could not be constructed from any of the twenty chromosomes.
These findings argue against a role for the founder mutation in the DYT1 gene in the etiology of occupational hand dystonia in this ethnic group.

findings.statement: Gasser et al. (1996) suggested that excessive repetitive use, possibly combined with ulnar neuropathy, may trigger some focal dystonias.
quotes: It appears that excessive, repetitive use, possibly in combination with ulnar neuropathy, may serve as the inciting cause of some focal dystonias.

relevance_reason: Linkage study of idiopathic torsion dystonia families in the UK and France. It supports a 9q34 (DYT1) locus in some families and shows genetic heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Warner et al. (1993) performed linkage analysis in 27 small families with idiopathic torsion dystonia (26 British and 1 French; 3 Ashkenazi Jewish), using the highly polymorphic 9q34 loci ASS and ABL. The cumulative lod score for ASS at a recombination fraction of 0.001 was -6.72. HOMOG analysis nevertheless gave evidence for linkage of an idiopathic torsion dystonia gene to 9q34 in a subset of families. The authors concluded that a locus at 9q34 exists in both Jewish and non-Jewish kindreds in the UK.
quotes: Linkage analysis was performed in 27 (26 British, one French) small families with idiopathic torsion dystonia, three of which were Ashkenazi Jewish, using the highly polymorphic loci argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and Abelson oncogene (ABL) which map to 9q34.
The cumulative lod score for the more informative ASS locus at a recombination fraction of 0.001 was -6.72.
indicate the existence of a locus for idiopathic torsion dystonia at 9q34 in both Jewish and non-Jewish kindreds in the UK.

findings.statement: Warner et al. (1993) found that lod scores in 3 non-Jewish families excluded a disease locus tightly linked to ASS on 9q34, although these families were clinically indistinguishable from the others. HOMOG analysis showed significant heterogeneity. The authors suggested that idiopathic torsion dystonia is genetically heterogeneous.
quotes: A large component of this score was derived from three non-Jewish families, indistinguishable clinically from the others, in which individual lod scores excluded a disease locus tightly linked to ASS.
Analysis of all the data using HOMOG showed significant heterogeneity
These data suggest genetic heterogeneity in idiopathic torsion dystonia

findings.statement: Warner et al. (1993) found the same allelic association between ASS/ABL and idiopathic torsion dystonia in British Jewish kindreds that had been reported in Ashkenazi Jewish families in the USA.
quotes: The allelic association observed between ASS/ABL and idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi families in the USA was also present in British Jewish kindreds.

relevance_reason: This is a linkage study showing that early limb-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in non-Jewish families maps to the DYT1 locus on 9q34. It also gives penetrance estimates and evidence that atypical dystonia involves other genes.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) studied 7 non-Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia of northern European and French Canadian descent. Their results were consistent with linkage to the DYT1 region on chromosome 9q34.
quotes: We examined seven non-Jewish ITD families of northern European and French Canadian descent to determine the extent to which early-onset ITD in non-Jews maps to DYT1. Results are consistent with linkage to the DYT1 region.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) found that affected members of 7 non-Jewish families linked to DYT1 were clinically similar to Ashkenazi Jewish cases. Onset was mainly in the limbs, and in each pedigree at least 1 person had onset before age 12 years.
quotes: Affected individuals in these families are clinically similar to the AJ cases; i.e., the site of onset is predominantly in the limbs and at least one individual in each pedigree had onset before age 12 years.

phenotypes.onset: before age 12 years in at least one individual per pedigree

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) reported that none of the affected individuals in the non-Jewish families carried the Ashkenazi Jewish DYT1 haplotype. They concluded that these families probably have different mutations in the DYT1 gene. The 2 French Canadian families shared the same haplotype.
quotes: None carries the AJ haplotype; therefore, they probably represent different mutations in the DYT1 gene. The two French Canadian families, however, display the same haplotype.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) estimated penetrance in the non-Jewish families at 0.40 to 0.75. After identifying disease gene carriers and adjusting for age at onset, they obtained a direct penetrance estimate of 0.46. This was consistent with the 30 to 40% estimated in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.
quotes: Estimates of penetrance in non-Jewish families range from .40 to .75. We identified disease gene carriers and, with adjustments for age at onset, obtained a direct estimate of penetrance of .46. This is consistent with estimates of 30%-40% in the AJ population.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) found that 2 other non-Jewish families with atypical idiopathic torsion dystonia, meaning later onset and/or cranial or cervical involvement, were not linked to DYT1. They took this as evidence that other genes are involved in dystonia.
quotes: Two other non-Jewish families with atypical ITD (later onset and/or cranial or cervical involvement) are not linked to DYT1, which indicates involvement of other genes in dystonia.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) noted that in the Ashkenazi Jewish population there is strong linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and nearby markers within a 2-cM region. The associated haplotype is present in more than 90% of early limb-onset Ashkenazi Jewish cases.
quotes: In the AJ population, strong linkage disequilibrium exists between DYT1 and adjacent markers within a 2-cM region. The associated haplotype occurs in > 90% of early limb-onset AJ cases.

relevance_reason: Clinical characterization of DYT1 founder-haplotype carriers vs noncarriers among Ashkenazi Jewish patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia.

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) studied 174 Ashkenazi Jewish individuals with idiopathic torsion dystonia, classifying them by a DYT1-associated haplotype of 9q34 markers (D9S62, D9S63, ASS) into 90 carriers, 70 noncarriers, and 14 ambiguous individuals. Mean age at onset was significantly lower in carriers than noncarriers (12.5 +/- 8.2 vs 36.5 +/- 16.4 years). In 94% of carriers symptoms began in a limb (arm or leg equally), and onset in the neck (3.3%) or larynx (2.2%) was rare.
quotes: There were 90 carriers, 70 noncarriers, and 14 ambiguous individuals.
The mean age at onset of symptoms was significantly lower in carriers than in noncarriers (12.5 +/- 8.2 vs 36.5 +/- 16.4 years).
In 94% of carriers, symptoms began in a limb (arm or leg equally); rarely the disorder started in the neck (3.3%) or larynx (2.2%).

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) found that among Ashkenazi Jewish dystonia patients not carrying the DYT1-associated haplotype, the neck, larynx, and other cranial muscles were the sites of onset in 79%, arm onset occurred in 21%, and leg onset never occurred. Limb onset, leg involvement during the disease course, and age at onset distinguished haplotype carriers from noncarriers with 90% accuracy.
quotes: In contrast, the neck, larynx, and other cranial muscles were the sites of onset in 79% of noncarriers; onset in the arms occurred in 21% and onset in the legs never occurred.
Limb onset, leg involvement in the course of disease, and age at onset distinguished haplotype carriers from noncarriers with 90% accuracy.

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) noted that linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and a particular 9q34 haplotype in Ashkenazi Jews implies that a large proportion of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in this population is due to a founder mutation in DYT1.
quotes: there is linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and a particular haplotype of alleles at 9q34 loci in this population. This implies that a large proportion of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews is due to a founder mutation in DYT1.

relevance_reason: Only the title ("Jewish diseases and origins") is available. It points to a general commentary on genetic diseases in Jewish populations, which may give population-genetics context for DYT1 in Ashkenazi Jews. However, the title itself says nothing about torsion dystonia, so no finding can be supported with a verbatim quote.
The paper describes a haplotype and founder-effect analysis of DYT1-linked early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jewish families on 9q34.

findings.statement: Risch et al. (1995) analyzed six closely linked microsatellite loci on chromosome 9q34 in 59 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia. They concluded that a single founder mutation accounts for most (more than 90%) of early-onset cases in the Ashkenazi population. They estimated that this mutation first appeared about 350 years ago.
quotes: We have examined data on six closely linked microsatellite loci on chromosome 9q34 from 59 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD).
Our data show that the vast majority (> 90%) of early-onset ITD cases in the Ashkenazi population are due to a single founder mutation, which we estimate first appeared approximately 350 years ago.

findings.statement: Risch et al. (1995) found that carriers of the founder mutation tended to come from the northern part of the historic Jewish Pale of Settlement (Lithuania and Byelorussia). They estimated the current frequency of this dominant mutation at between 1/6,000 and 1/2,000. They suggested that the mutation's recent origin and high frequency mean the Ashkenazi population descends from a limited group of founders, and they emphasized the role of genetic drift.
quotes: We also show that carriers preferentially originate from the northern part of the historic Jewish Pale of settlement (Lithuania and Byelorussia).

The recent origin of this dominant mutation and its current high frequency (between 1/6,000 and 1/2,000) suggest that the Ashkenazi population descends from a limited group of founders, and emphasize the importance of genetic drift

relevance_reason: Only the title was available. It shows the paper discusses whether genetic drift or selection explains idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in Ashkenazi Jews, a population-genetics question relevant to DYT1.

findings.statement: Zoossmann-Diskin (1995) discussed whether genetic drift or selection accounts for idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.
quotes: ITD in Ashkenazi Jews--genetic drift or selection?

relevance_reason: The abstract reports serum DBH activity and a metoclopramide provocative test in Ashkenazi Jewish patients with torsion dystonia and their relatives. This is biochemical evidence a curator could cite in the DYT1 entry.

findings.statement: Askenasy et al. (1980) studied 13 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with torsion dystonia of various origins, together with their families. Patients and their relatives had significantly higher serum dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (DBH) activity than controls, particularly in the childhood-onset group. Jewish origin, dominant inheritance, slow progression and axial distribution were each not specific for an elevated serum DBH activity.
quotes: A familial study of 13 Ashkenasy Jewish patients suffering from torsion dystonia (TD) of various origin
A significantly high serum DBH activity was found in TD patients and their relatives compared with controls, particularly in the childhood onset group.
None of the following criteria: Jewish origin, dominant trait, slow progression and axial topography are specific for an elevated serum DBH activity.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Abnormal circulating enzyme concentration or activity

findings.statement: Askenasy et al. (1980) found that an intravenous injection of 20 mg metoclopramide did not change serum DBH activity in 12 patients with torsion dystonia or in 17 relatives. In 1 patient with symptomatic dystonia and 2 of her maternal relatives (who had different fathers), serum DBH activity doubled or tripled after the injection. The authors suggested that a metoclopramide-induced rise in serum DBH activity in relatives of torsion dystonia patients indicates a genetic predisposition.
quotes: Intravenous injection of 20 mg Metoclopramide (MP) did not change serum DBH activity in 12 patients and 17 relatives.

In one patient with symptomatic dystonia and two of her maternal relatives (from different fathers) serum DBH activity increased after i.v. injection of MP. In these three cases the serum DBH activity doubled and tripled.
It is suggested that the MP induced elevation of serum DBH activity in relatives of TD patients indicates a genetic disposition.

relevance_reason: Title indicates a study of the inheritance pattern of torsion dystonia in Jewish populations, directly relevant to DYT1; only the title is available, so no details can be extracted.

findings.statement: Eldridge (1981) addressed the mode of inheritance of torsion dystonia in Jews.
quotes: Inheritance of torsion dystonia in Jews.

Epidemiologic and segregation analysis of idiopathic torsion dystonia in Israeli Jews. It reports frequency among Ashkenazi/European Jews and supports autosomal dominant inheritance with low penetrance.

findings.statement: Zilber et al. (1984) analyzed data from a nationwide survey of idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in Israel. They identified 47 patients between 1969 and 1980, 40 of them of European origin. Among European Jews, ITD frequency was about 1 in 23,000 live births, about 5 times higher than in Jews of Afro-Asian origin.
quotes: Between 1969 and 1980, 47 patients were collected, of whom 40 were of European origin.
In these European Jews, the ITD frequency was about 1:23 000 live births, which was five-fold greater than in Jews of Afro-Asian origin.

findings.statement: Zilber et al. (1984) assumed that all ITD cases in their Israeli Jewish series fit one genetic model. Under that assumption, X-linked and simple autosomal recessive models did not fit the data well. An autosomal dominant model with low penetrance could account for the observations and gave an estimated ITD gene frequency of 3 to 4 per 100,000 in European Jews. Multifactorial inheritance was also possible. The authors cautioned that it may be inappropriate to assume all cases share the same genetic basis, or even that all are inherited.
quotes: an X linked or a simple autosomal recessive model of inheritance did not agree well with our data
An autosomal dominant model with low penetrance could have accounted for our observations and would yield an ITD gene frequency in European Jews of 3 to 4:100 000.
Multifactorial inheritance was also possible. However, it may be inappropriate to assume that all cases have the same genetic basis, or even that all are inherited.

findings.statement: Zilber et al. (1984) found that fathers of isolated ITD cases were older than expected. Based on this, they suggested that some isolated cases may have been new mutations.
quotes: In view of the increased ages of their fathers, the isolated cases may have included some new mutations.

relevance_reason: Describes a rat mutant (dt) proposed as an animal model of dystonia musculorum deformans; animal model section.

findings.statement: Lorden et al. (1984) described an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder, named dystonic (dt), in Sprague-Dawley rats, characterized by sustained twisting movements during waking. Mutants were indistinguishable from normal littermates before postnatal days 9 to 10; signs beginning on day 10 included twisting of the axial musculature, hyperflexion of the trunk, self-clasping of forelimbs and hindlimbs, and poor limb placement during locomotion. No morphologic lesions of neural or non-neural tissues were seen with routine light microscopy.
quotes: The mutation follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance and has been named dystonic (dt).

Clinical signs begin to appear on day 10 and include twisting of the axial musculature, hyperflexion of the trunk, self-clasping of forelimbs and hindlimbs, and poor placement of the limbs during locomotion.
No morphological lesions of neural or non-neural tissues have been observed with routine light microscopy.

phenotypes.text: poor placement of limbs during locomotion

findings.statement: Lorden et al. (1984) found that dt rats had significantly elevated cerebellar norepinephrine levels, with normal levels in other locus ceruleus terminal fields and no difference in cerebellar noradrenergic innervation by histochemical fluorescence. The mutants were less sensitive to the akinesic effects of haloperidol, although striatal dopamine levels were not reliably different and apomorphine responses appeared normal. The authors suggested biochemical disturbances in the extrapyramidal system and proposed the dt rat as a model for human dystonia musculorum deformans.
quotes: Dystonic rats demonstrate significantly elevated cerebellar norepinephrine levels, although levels in other terminal fields of the locus ceruleus are similar to those of normal littermates.
These mutants were less sensitive than unaffected littermates to the akinesic effects of the dopamine blocker haloperidol.
These findings suggest the presence of biochemical disturbances in the extrapyramidal system of dt rats. The dt rat may provide a useful model for human dystonia musculorum deformans.

findings.statement: Zeman and Dyken (1967) reported clinical, genetic and pathoanatomical studies of dystonia musculorum deformans.
quotes: Dystonia musculorum deformans. Clinical, genetic and pathoanatomical studies.

findings.statement: Yanagisawa et al. (1972) reported familial dystonia musculorum deformans occurring together with tremor.
quotes: Familial dystonia musculorum deformans and tremor.
