findings.statement: Batshaw et al. (1985) reported that Munchausen's syndrome can simulate torsion dystonia, which makes it a consideration in the differential diagnosis.
quotes: Munchausen's syndrome simulating torsion dystonia.

relevance_reason: Exclusion mapping of the autosomal dominant torsion dystonia gene in a large non-Jewish pedigree; adds mapping (exclusion) evidence.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1987) performed multipoint linkage analysis of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia in a single large non-Jewish pedigree using linkage groups on chromosomes 11p, 13q, and 21q. They excluded large portions of chromosomes 11p and 13q and virtually the entire long arm of chromosome 21 from linkage with dystonia.
quotes: Analyses are based on family data from a single, large, non-Jewish pedigree.
Large portions of chromosomes 11p and 13q, and virtually the entire long arm of chromosome 21 are excluded from linkage with dystonia.

relevance_reason: Linkage exclusion study in a large family with autosomal dominant torsion dystonia; excludes POMC and GAD candidate genes and other genomic regions.

findings.statement: Breakefield et al. (1986) performed linkage analysis with restriction fragment length polymorphisms in a family with autosomal dominant torsion dystonia in which more than 50 members had neurologic examination. Using LOD score analysis that allowed for age of onset and incomplete penetrance, they excluded the pro-opiomelanocortin and glutamic acid decarboxylase genes, which had been implicated in rat models, as well as other genomic regions, as the site of the disease gene in this family.
quotes: Complete neurologic examination and establishment of lymphoblast lines have been carried out for over 50 members.

Genes for pro-opiomelanocortin and glutamic acid decarboxylase, which have been implicated in the etiology of the disease in rat models, were excluded as being responsible for the disease state in this family.
Other regions of the genome were also excluded using DNA probes for other genes and random "unique" sequences.

findings.statement: Breakefield et al. (1986) studied a family in which torsion dystonia showed autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.
quotes: A search for the defective gene causing torsion dystonia has been carried out in a family manifesting an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance of this movement disorder.
with requisite assumptions for mode of inheritance, age-of-onset and incomplete gene penetrance

relevance_reason: Family segregation analysis showing that idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with reduced penetrance; this bears directly on the inheritance of DYT1.

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (1989) studied the families of 43 Ashkenazi Jewish probands whose idiopathic torsion dystonia began before age 28 years. They examined 146 first-degree and 96 second-degree relatives; 19 relatives had definite dystonia and 2 had probable dystonia. Counting definite cases only, the age-adjusted risk was 15.5% for first-degree relatives and 6.5% for second-degree relatives. Risk did not differ significantly by sex, or between parents, offspring and sibs. Using maximum likelihood analysis, the authors found the risks consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance, with penetrance estimated at 29.4% for definite cases or 32.2% when probable cases were included.
quotes: We studied 43 probands, 146 (90.1%) of 162 living first-degree relatives, and 96 (40.2%) of 239 living second-degree relatives. Nineteen relatives had definite dystonia, and 2 had probable dystonia.

Using definite cases only, the age-adjusted risk for all first-degree relatives was 15.5% and for all second-degree relatives 6.5%, with no significant sex differences; parent, offspring, and sibling risks did not differ significantly.
The risks were consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with a penetrance estimated at 29.4% using definite cases only or 32.2% using definite and probable cases.

findings.statement: Assuming a disease frequency of 1 in 15,000 among Ashkenazi Jews, Bressman et al. (1989) estimated the gene frequency for idiopathic torsion dystonia at 1 in 9,000.
quotes: Assuming a disease frequency of 1/15,000, the gene frequency was estimated to be 1/9000.

relevance_reason: This is the first linkage study to map the gene for autosomal dominant torsion dystonia (DYT1) to chromosome 9q32-q34.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) used linkage analysis with polymorphic DNA and protein markers in a large non-Jewish kindred with torsion dystonia. They found that the dystonia gene (ITD1) was tightly linked to the gelsolin gene. Multipoint linkage analysis placed it in the 9q32-q34 region, between ABO and D9S26, a region that also contains the dopamine-beta-hydroxylase locus.
quotes: linkage analysis using polymorphic DNA and protein markers has been used to locate a gene responsible for susceptibility to dystonia in a large, non-Jewish kinship

This dystonia gene (ITD1) shows tight linkage with the gene encoding gelsolin, an actin binding protein, and appears by multipoint linkage analysis to lie in the q32-q34 region of chromosome 9 between ABO and D9S26

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) reported that affected members of a large non-Jewish kindred with torsion dystonia had a clinical syndrome similar to the one seen in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. Torsion dystonia is characterized by loss of control of voluntary movements, appearing as sustained muscle contractions and/or abnormal postures.
quotes: Affected members of this family have a clinical syndrome similar to that found in the Jewish population.
characterized by loss of control of voluntary movements appearing as sustained muscle contractions and/or abnormal postures

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) noted that most of the hereditary forms of torsion dystonia described so far show autosomal dominant transmission with variable expressivity.
quotes: Several hereditary forms have been described, most of which have autosomal dominant transmission with variable expressivity.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) stated that the frequency of the defective torsion dystonia gene in the Ashkenazi Jewish population is about 1 in 10,000.
quotes: In the Ashkenazi Jewish population the defective gene frequency is about 1/10,000.

relevance_reason: Postmortem neuropathologic and neurochemical study of the brains of patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans. It adds biochemical and pathogenesis evidence relevant to DYT1.

findings.statement: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) examined the brains of 2 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans after death. Histology showed no important changes in the basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, higher brainstem nuclei, locus ceruleus, or raphe nuclei. Choline acetyltransferase activity and the levels of GABA and glutamic acid in the cortex and basal ganglia were within the control range. Norepinephrine concentrations were markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. Serotonin was subnormal in the dorsal raphe nucleus, dopamine was low in the nucleus accumbens (and in the striatum in 1 of the 2 cases), and norepinephrine, serotonin, and 5-HIAA were raised in several other regions.
quotes: We examined histologically and biochemically the brains of two patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans. We found no important histologic changes in the basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, higher brain-stem nuclei, locus ceruleus, or raphe nuclei.
In contrast, the norepinephrine concentrations were markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus.
The serotonin level was subnormal in the dorsal raphe nucleus, as was the dopamine level in the nucleus accumbens and, in one of the two cases, in the striatum.

phenotypes.text: decreased brain norepinephrine in hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus

findings.statement: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) concluded that some of the monoamine changes they found may represent a basic neurochemical abnormality in dystonia musculorum deformans, especially the pronounced apparent disturbance of noradrenergic brain mechanisms. They suggested these changes may be relevant to the disorder's pathophysiology and treatment.
quotes: We conclude that some of these monoamine changes, especially the pronounced apparent disturbance of noradrenergic brain mechanisms, may represent a basic neurochemical abnormality in dystonia musculorum deformans and may thus be relevant to the pathoneurophysiology and treatment of this disorder.

relevance_reason: A review of the genetics of primary torsion dystonia. It summarizes the inheritance modes, clinical heterogeneity of the autosomal dominant forms, and the assignment of a torsion dystonia locus to 9q. It reports no new patients or variants.

findings.statement: In a review, Müller and Kupke (1990) stated that primary torsion dystonia may be inherited as an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive trait, and that at least six forms of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia can be distinguished clinically.
quotes: The disorder may be inherited either as an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive trait.
At least six forms of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia can be distinguished clinically.

findings.statement: Müller and Kupke (1990) reviewed linkage analysis in one form of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia that assigned a 'torsion dystonia locus' to the long arm of chromosome 9.
quotes: Linkage analysis in one form of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia permits the assignment of a "torsion dystonia locus" to the long arm of chromosome 9.

findings.statement: Müller and Kupke (1990) described primary torsion dystonia as an idiopathic movement disorder presumably caused by abnormal function of the basal ganglia.
quotes: Primary torsion dystonia is an idiopathic movement disorder presumably caused by abnormal function of the basal ganglia.

relevance_reason: Linkage mapping of the dystonia gene (DYT1) to 9q32-34 in Ashkenazi Jewish families.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) used linkage analysis with DNA polymorphisms in 12 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD). They found that the dystonia gene was closely linked to the argininosuccinate synthetase gene (ASS). Multipoint analysis placed it in the 9q32-q34 region, which also contains the gelsolin and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase loci.
quotes: linkage analysis using DNA polymorphisms is used to locate a gene responsible for susceptibility to ITD in 12 Ashkenazi Jewish families
This dystonia gene exhibits close linkage with the gene encoding argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS), and appears by multipoint analysis to lie in the q32-34 region of chromosome 9

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) suggested that the same gene may cause ITD both in a previously reported non-Jewish kindred linked to 9q32-34 and in the Ashkenazi Jewish families they studied. Because penetrance of the dominant allele differed substantially between the 2 groups, they suggested that 2 different mutations may produce susceptibility to the disease in the 2 groups.
quotes: The same gene may be responsible for ITD both in the non-Jewish kindred mentioned above and in the Ashkenazi Jewish families presented here.

because there is substantial difference between the penetrance of the dominant allele in these two groups, two different mutations may be operating to produce susceptibility to this disease in the two groups

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) noted that ITD is 5 to 10 times more frequent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population than in other groups.
quotes: The frequency of ITD in the Ashkenazi Jewish population is five to ten times greater than that in other groups.

findings.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) described idiopathic torsion dystonia as a neurologic disorder of sustained muscle contractions. These appear as twisting movements of the limbs, trunk, and/or neck and can progress to abnormal postures. Most familial forms follow autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance.
quotes: Idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) is a neurological disorder characterized by sustained muscle contractions that appear as twisting movements of the limbs, trunk, and/or neck, which can progress to abnormal postures.
Most familial forms of ITD follow autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance.

phenotypes.text: sustained muscle contractions with twisting movements

relevance_reason: Segregation analysis that established autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance for early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews.

findings.statement: Risch et al. (1990) carried out segregation analysis in a family study of idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews. The study included 43 probands with onset before age 27 years from 42 nuclear families. The pedigrees were extended through all available first- and second-degree relatives, who were examined directly and videotaped. Final diagnoses were based on the examination findings and a blinded review of the videotapes. The data were consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with 30% penetrance. Recessive and polygenic inheritance were strongly rejected, and there was no evidence for sporadic cases or new mutations.
quotes: The study is based on 43 probands (with age at onset prior to 27 years) from 42 nuclear families; pedigrees were extended systematically through all available first- and second-degree relatives, who were directly examined and videotaped.
Segregation analysis demonstrated that the data are consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with 30% penetrance. Recessive and polygenic inheritance were strongly rejected.
There was no evidence for sporadic cases or new mutations.

findings.statement: Risch et al. (1990) suggested that the high incidence and dominant inheritance of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews pointed to genetic homogeneity within this population. They proposed that this would make the population especially useful for linkage studies.
quotes: The high incidence and dominant inheritance of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews suggests genetic homogeneity within this population, making it especially useful for linkage studies of this disorder.

relevance_reason: Linkage study that narrows the DYT1 locus on 9q32-34 in Ashkenazi Jewish families and in a non-Jewish family.

findings.statement: Using GT repeat polymorphisms from the 9q32-34 region, Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) localized the gene causing idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jewish families to the 11-cM interval between AK1 and D9S10. The authors stated that no candidate genes were known in this region.
quotes: Utilizing GT repeat polymorphisms from this region, here we demonstrate that the gene causing dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews can be localized to the 11-cM interval between AK1 and D9S10.
Currently there are no known candidate genes in this region.

findings.statement: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) found that linkage analysis in a large non-Jewish family was also consistent with the dystonia gene lying in the 9q32-34 region, although positive lod scores in that family extended over an interval of more than 20 cM.
quotes: Linkage analysis in the non-Jewish family is also consistent with occurrence of the gene in this region, although positive lod scores extend over a greater than 20-cM interval in that family.

findings.statement: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) described idiopathic torsion dystonia as sustained, involuntary muscle contractions that often cause twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures. They noted that most familial forms show autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance.
quotes: Idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) is characterized by sustained, involuntary muscle contractions, frequently causing twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures.
Most familial forms of ITD display autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance.

relevance_reason: Fine mapping of DYT1 and linkage disequilibrium in Ashkenazi Jewish patients with early-onset torsion dystonia; founder effect, penetrance and inheritance evidence.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) used (GT)n and RFLP markers on chromosome 9q32-34 and identified obligate recombination events in Ashkenazi Jewish families with early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia, narrowing the DYT1 region to a 6-cM interval bounded by AK1 and ASS. Based on obligate recombinants, DYT1 was placed centromeric to ASS, and allelic association predicted that DYT1, ABL, and ASS lie within 1-2 cM of each other.
quotes: we have identified obligate recombination events in some of these Jewish families, which further delineate the area containing the DYT1 gene to a 6-cM region bounded by loci AK1 and ASS

The allelic association between this extended haplotype and DYT1 predicts that these three genes lie within 1-2 cM of each other; on the basis of obligate recombination events, the DYT1 gene is centromeric to ASS.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) found highly significant linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and an extended ABL-ASS haplotype in 52 unrelated affected Ashkenazi Jewish individuals: the 4/A12 haplotype was present on 69% of disease-bearing chromosomes versus 1% of control Jewish chromosomes (chi-square = 91.07). The authors concluded that a single mutation event is responsible for most hereditary cases of dystonia in the Jewish population.
quotes: In 52 unrelated, affected Ashkenazi Jewish individuals, we have found highly significant linkage disequilibrium between a particular extended haplotype at the ABL-ASS loci and the DYT1 gene.

The 4/A12 haplotype for ABL-ASS is present on 69% of the disease-bearing chromosomes among affected Jewish individuals and on only 1% of control Jewish chromosomes (chi 2 = 91.07, P much less than .001).
this allelic association supports the idea that a single mutation event is responsible for most hereditary cases of dystonia in the Jewish population

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) found that of 53 definitely affected Ashkenazi Jewish individuals typed, 13 appeared sporadic, yet a similar proportion of sporadic (8/13, 62%) and familial (28/40, 70%) cases carried the ASS A12 haplotype. They suggested that many sporadic cases are hereditary, that the disease gene frequency is greater than 1/15,000, and that penetrance is lower than the previously estimated 30%; most affected individuals were heterozygous for the ABL-ASS haplotype, supporting autosomal dominant inheritance.
quotes: Of the 53 definitely affected typed, 13 appear to be sporadic, with no family history of dystonia. However, the proportion of sporadic cases which potentially carry the A12 haplotype at ASS (8/13 [62%]) is similar to the proportion of familial cases with A12 (28/40 [70%]).
This suggests that many sporadic cases are hereditary, that the disease gene frequency is greater than 1/15,000, and that the penetrance is lower than 30%, as previously estimated in this population.
Most affected individuals were heterozygous for the ABL-ASS haplotype, a finding supporting autosomal dominant inheritance of the DYT1 gene.

findings.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) proposed that ABL-ASS extended-haplotype status would provide predictive value for DYT1 carrier status in Jewish individuals and could be used for molecular diagnosis.
quotes: The ABL-ASS extended-haplotype status will provide predictive value for carrier status in Jewish individuals. This information can be used for molecular diagnosis

relevance_reason: Early family study of torsion dystonia showing that there are autosomal dominant forms (with childhood or adult onset), a paternal age effect in sporadic cases, and reduced fitness. This is relevant to the inheritance and heterogeneity of DYT1.

findings.statement: Bundey et al. (1975) carried out a family study of 32 patients with torsion dystonia. They identified at least 2 forms of generalized dystonia with onset in childhood, one autosomal dominant and one autosomal recessive, and the 2 forms could not be told apart clinically. At least 3 families and probably about 6 to 8 patients had the autosomal recessive form.
quotes: A family study of 32 patients with torsion dystonia has shown at least two forms of generalized dystonia with onset in childhood. These two forms, an autosomal dominant and an autosomal recessive, are clinically indistinguishable.
There were at least three families and probably about six to eight patients with the autosomal recessive variety.

findings.statement: Bundey et al. (1975) suggested that the remaining 9 to 11 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia were new dominant mutations, because there appeared to be a paternal age effect. Since fitness in patients with childhood onset was 1/20 of normal, most childhood dominant cases appeared sporadically.
quotes: The remaining nine to 11 patients with generalized childhood dystonia are thought, because of a probable paternal age effect, to be examples of new dominant mutations.
Since fitness with childhood onset is 1/20 of normal, most childhood dominant cases appear sporadically.

findings.statement: Bundey et al. (1975) found that most of the other 15 patients, 12 of whom had onset in adult life, appeared to have a non-genetic torsion dystonia. However, they observed one example of a benign adult-onset dominant form associated with tremor. They concluded that there are at least 2 genetic forms of torsion dystonia: an autosomal recessive childhood-onset form and one or more dominant forms with onset in childhood or adult life.
quotes: Most of the other 15 patients (12 with onset in adult life) appear to have a non-genetic torsion dystonia, although an example of a benign adult-onset dominant form associated with a tremor has been observed.

It is concluded that there are at least two forms of genetic torsion dystonia, an autosomal recessive form with onset in childhood, which, on evidence from America, is particularly common in Ashkenazi Jews, and one or more dominant forms, with onset in childhood or adult life.
